planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in late winter; Moneymaker is a Type I pollinator and benefits from a nearby Type II variety such as Stuart for cross-pollination and improved yields.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, with a compatible pollinizer variety nearby for the best nut set. Moneymaker is an early 20th-century Texas pecan valued above all for its dependable, consistent annual production, avoiding the pronounced alternate-year bearing pattern (heavy crop one year, light the next) that plagues many other pecan varieties and makes yields far less predictable. The medium-sized nuts have a thin shell and good kernel quality, and the tree shows solid resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that is the single biggest production challenge for pecans in humid Southern climates. Because of its reliability, Moneymaker has remained a popular choice for home orchards over more than a century, even as many showier, larger-nutted varieties have come and gone. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, and expect the first significant nut crops five to seven years after planting.

Shawnee is a USDA-released pecan bred for good resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that causes the most serious losses in humid, high-rainfall pecan-growing regions, combined with notably precocious bearing, meaning young trees begin producing meaningful nut crops earlier than many older varieties. The medium to large nuts have good kernel quality and ripen relatively early in the fall, an advantage in areas where hurricane season or early frost can threaten a late-ripening crop still on the tree. The moderately vigorous tree is well suited to home orchards wanting a scab-resistant option without the extreme size of some larger pecan cultivars. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, and expect the first significant crops within five to seven years of planting.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Independence is a widely grown California nectarine prized for its brilliant, nearly solid red skin and firm, richly flavored yellow flesh, ripening in midsummer on a vigorous, productive tree. The freestone pit and firm texture make it easy to prepare fresh or for preserving, and the fruit's excellent eating quality has kept it a standard commercial and home-orchard variety for decades. Like all nectarines, it shares peach genetics closely enough to suffer the same pest and disease pressures — particularly brown rot and peach leaf curl — so a routine dormant-season spray program is important for a clean crop. Thin fruit to four to six inches apart after natural drop for the best size and flavor.

common_name: Double Delight Nectarine (Showy Double-Flowering Ornamental Fruiting Nectarine)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile and needs no pollinizer; best adapted to zones 5-9.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Double Delight is grown as much for its spectacular spring floral display as for its fruit, opening large, fully double, deep pink blossoms that rival an ornamental flowering peach or cherry before setting a genuinely good crop of sweet, white-fleshed, freestone nectarines in summer. This dual-purpose ornamental-and-edible quality makes it a popular choice for home landscapes wanting a fruit tree that earns its space as a spring showpiece as well as a producer. Like other nectarines, the smooth skin makes it more susceptible to brown rot and other fungal issues than fuzzy-skinned peaches, so a dormant-season spray program helps protect both the spectacular bloom and the eventual fruit crop. Thin fruit after natural drop for the best size and flavor.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Harko was bred at the Harrow research station in Ontario, Canada specifically to extend nectarine growing into colder climates than most varieties can tolerate, combining genuine cold hardiness with good resistance to bacterial spot, a disease that troubles many nectarines in humid regions. The medium-sized fruit has bright red skin over yellow, firm, freestone flesh with good sweet-tart flavor, ripening in midsummer on a reliably productive tree. Its combination of hardiness and disease tolerance has made it a popular choice for home orchardists in the northern half of nectarine-growing range who still want good eating quality without the extra winter losses less hardy varieties suffer. Thin fruit after natural drop, and maintain routine brown rot management common to all nectarines.
